---
title: "Figure 11.2: Monetary and Fiscal Policy, 2024–26 (Brazil, Colombia, Mexico)"
---

![Python: `python/fig-11-2.py`](../images/python/fig-11-2.png)

The same policy-mix chart as [Figure 11.1](fig-11-1.qmd), for Brazil,
Colombia and Mexico. Each country is a path through three years, 2024 to
2026. The horizontal position is the fiscal stance (the change in the
structural primary balance: right is tightening), the vertical position the
monetary stance (the real policy rate minus the neutral rate: up is
tightening). The four quadrants are labelled with the policy mix they stand
for, from "expansionary fiscal, contractionary monetary" in the top left to
"contractionary fiscal, expansionary monetary" in the bottom right.

Read the Figure 11.1 page first: it explains every step of the script. This
page recaps the structure and then goes through the settings that differ.

## The data

Sheet `data`, 9 rows: three years for each of three countries, in the same
long format as Figure 11.1. Each row is one point, with columns `series`
(the country code), `x` and `y`. The script selects a country's three rows
with `data[data["series"] == country]`.

## The script in brief

The script has the same five parts as Figure 11.1:

1. **The paths.** For each country, `smooth_line()` draws a curve through
   its three points, as Excel's smoothed scatter line does. The last three
   points of the curve are left off the line and replaced by an arrowhead
   drawn with `ax.annotate()`, so the arrow shows the direction of time. The
   three yearly points are then drawn on top as white dots with a coloured
   edge (`ax.scatter(..., facecolor="white", edgecolor=colour)`).
2. **Axes that cross at zero.** The left and bottom spines are hidden, and
   lines at x = 0 and y = 0 are drawn instead, with their own tick marks.
   The scale labels stay at the left and bottom edges.
3. **Axis titles**, set with `ax.set_xlabel()` and `ax.set_ylabel()`, each
   on two lines.
4. **Quadrant labels** in grey italics, one in each corner.
5. **A legend** with a line and a white dot for each country.

## What differs from Figure 11.1

| | Figure 11.1 | Figure 11.2 |
|---|---|---|
| Countries | USA, CAN | BRA, COL, MEX |
| x-axis | -1 to 2 | -3 to 2 |
| y-axis | -1 to 1.5, step 0.5, one decimal | -1 to 7, step 1, whole numbers |
| Line width | 2.0 | 2.2 |
| Legend | upper left, near the middle | right, vertically centred |

### Countries and colours

```python
series_colours = {"BRA": "#63277F", "COL": "#D05A08", "MEX": "#66696A"}
```

Three countries instead of two. The loop over `series_colours` draws one
path per entry, so nothing else in the drawing code has to change. The
legend is built from the same dictionary and also gets three entries.

### The scales

```python
ax.set_xlim(-3, 2)
ax.set_xticks(range(-3, 3))
ax.set_ylim(-1, 7)
ax.set_yticks(range(-1, 8))
```

The Latin American countries had much larger policy rate gaps than the
United States and Canada, up to about 6 percentage points, and larger fiscal
changes. Both ranges are therefore wider. With whole-number steps, the
y-labels need no decimal, so the one-decimal formatter of Figure 11.1 is
gone.

`range(-3, 3)` gives -3, -2, ..., 2; `range(-1, 8)` gives -1, 0, ..., 7. A
range stops before its second number.

### The tick marks on the axis lines

The tick marks on the lines at zero must match the scale:

```python
ax.vlines([-3, -2, -1, 1, 2], 0, 0.14, color="black", linewidth=0.6)
ax.hlines(range(-1, 8), 0, 0.055, color="black", linewidth=0.6)
```

- `ax.vlines(x, ymin, ymax)` draws short vertical marks on the horizontal
  line at y = 0, at each x-label except 0. At x = 0 the vertical axis line
  itself is the mark.
- `ax.hlines(y, xmin, xmax)` draws short horizontal marks on the vertical
  line at x = 0, one per y-label.

The tick length is in data units, so it is longer here than in Figure 11.1:

- **On the x-axis line**, ticks are 0.14 high, against a y-range of 8, so
  1.75 percent of the plot height.
- **On the y-axis line**, ticks are 0.055 wide, against an x-range of 5, so
  about 1.1 percent of the plot width.

The plot is taller than it is wide in data terms, and the two percentages
are chosen so the marks look about equally long on screen. Whenever you
change a scale in this kind of chart, recompute the tick length as roughly
the same fraction of the new range. See [An axis line at
zero](../techniques.qmd#sec-axis-line).

### The quadrant labels

The quadrant labels move to the new corners:

```python
quadrants = [
    (-2.95, 7.0, "left", "top", "Exp FP\nCon MP"),
    (1.95, 7.0, "right", "top", "Con FP\nCon MP"),
    (-2.95, -1.0, "left", "bottom", "Exp FP\nExp MP"),
    (1.95, -1.0, "right", "bottom", "Con FP\nExp MP"),
]
```

Each entry gives the position (x, y), the horizontal and vertical
alignment, and the text. The positions are the corners of the plot, moved
0.05 inwards horizontally so the text does not touch the edge. The alignment
makes each label grow away from its corner: the top-left label is aligned
by its top-left point, the bottom-right one by its bottom-right point, and so
on. A loop then writes all four with `ax.text()`. See [Text, arrows and
coordinates](../techniques.qmd#sec-text).

### Thicker lines and the legend

The paths are 2.2 points wide instead of 2.0, as in the published chart.
The legend moves to the right edge, vertically centred
(`loc="center right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5)`), because at the place where Figure 11.1 has
it, near the top middle, it would cover part of the Brazilian path, which
reaches 6 in 2025.

The frame is also different: `left=0.8` and `bottom_gap=0.65` leave room for
the two-line axis titles.

## A possible improvement

Two scripts that differ only in their settings are a sign that the shared
code could become a function, as was done for the R versions. A
`policy_mix_chart(stem, colours, subtitle, xlim, ylim, ...)` would let both
charts be drawn from the same code, and compute the tick lengths and
quadrant positions from the limits. The Python scripts are kept separate, so
each chart can be read on its own.

## The complete script

The full `python/fig-11-2.py`, as it runs:

```` {.python filename="python/fig-11-2.py"}
"""Figure 11.2: Monetary and Fiscal Policy, 2024–26 (Brazil, Colombia, Mexico)."""
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from chart_style import new_chart, read_chart_data, save_chart, smooth_line

STEM = "fig-11-2"

data = read_chart_data(STEM)

series_colours = {"BRA": "#63277F", "COL": "#D05A08", "MEX": "#66696A"}

fig, ax = new_chart(
    title="Monetary and Fiscal Policy, 2024–26",
    subtitle="(Brazil, Colombia, Mexico)",
    caption=(
        "Sources: Consensus Economics; Haver Analytics; IMF, World Economic\n"
        "Outlook database; and IMF staff calculations.\n"
        "Note: The real ex ante policy rate gap is the difference between the real\n"
        "ex ante policy rate and the real neutral rate. The real ex ante policy rate is\n"
        "the difference between the nominal policy rate and the 1-year ahead\n"
        "inflation expectations. Con = contractionary; Exp = expansionary; MP =\n"
        "monetary policy; FP = fiscal policy."
    ),
    left=0.8,
    right=0.25,
    bottom_gap=0.65,
)

# Each country moves through three years (2024, 2025, 2026). The path is a
# smoothed line, as in Excel, with an arrow showing the direction.
for country, colour in series_colours.items():
    path = data[data["series"] == country]
    xs, ys = smooth_line(path["x"], path["y"])
    ax.plot(xs[:-3], ys[:-3], color=colour, linewidth=2.2)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(xs[-1], ys[-1]), xytext=(xs[-4], ys[-4]),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=colour, linewidth=2.2,
                                mutation_scale=12, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=4))
    ax.scatter(path["x"], path["y"], s=40, facecolor="white", edgecolor=colour,
               linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)

# Axes cross at zero; the scale labels stay at the left and bottom edges.
for side in ("left", "bottom"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
ax.vlines([-3, -2, -1, 1, 2], 0, 0.14, color="black", linewidth=0.6)
ax.hlines(range(-1, 8), 0, 0.055, color="black", linewidth=0.6)
ax.tick_params(length=0, pad=5)

ax.set_xlim(-3, 2)
ax.set_xticks(range(-3, 3))
ax.set_ylim(-1, 7)
ax.set_yticks(range(-1, 8))
ax.set_xlabel("Change in structural primary balance\n(percentage points of potential GDP)",
              fontsize=9, labelpad=4)
ax.set_ylabel("Real ex ante policy rate gap\n(percentage points)", fontsize=9,
              labelpad=4)

# Quadrant labels.
quadrants = [
    (-2.95, 7.0, "left", "top", "Exp FP\nCon MP"),
    (1.95, 7.0, "right", "top", "Con FP\nCon MP"),
    (-2.95, -1.0, "left", "bottom", "Exp FP\nExp MP"),
    (1.95, -1.0, "right", "bottom", "Con FP\nExp MP"),
]
for qx, qy, ha, va, label in quadrants:
    ax.text(qx, qy, label, ha=ha, va=va, color="#777777", fontstyle="italic",
            fontsize=8.5, linespacing=1.0)

ax.legend(
    [Line2D([], [], color=c, linewidth=2.2, marker="o", markersize=5,
            markerfacecolor="white") for c in series_colours.values()],
    list(series_colours),
    loc="center right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5), handlelength=2.6,
    labelspacing=0.2,
)

save_chart(fig, STEM)
````
